newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban advance into Panjsher valley.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban advance into Panjsher valley.

text.p: Afghanistan's hardline Islamist Taleban militia launched a major assault on the Panjsher valley stronghold of former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood on Saturday, taking two hills at the entrance to the valley, witnesses said.
As helicopter gunships, anti-aircraft batteries and BM-21 rocket launchers pounded Masood's defences, turban-clad warriors clawed their way up rocky scree onto the newly-captured hills.
"We have already advanced and God willing we will take the whole valley," Mullah Raz Mohammad Ali Jay, a Taleban commander, told Reuters.
Taleban fighters marched past the narrow entrance to the rocky gorge that leads into the valley, but took cover or retreated as Masood's forces fired back with ZU-23 anti-aircraft guns.

The attack, the first on the valley since the Taleban took over the capital Kabul with little fighting just over a week ago, began before dawn as fighters launched volleys of rockets on well-entrenched positions inside the winding gorge.
The Taleban have won control of about three-quarters of the country in the two years since the movement was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Afghanistan.
Taleban leaders had told Masood to surrender or be cleared out of the valley to which he retreated in disarray after the Sunni militia, composed mainly of ethnic Pashtuns, took Kabul.
There has been no reply from Masood, who defended the mainly Tajik-populated valley against Soviet forces who backed a communist government in Kabul during the 1980s.

Soviet forces used bombers and helicopter landings in vain attempts to capture the Panjsher in battles that won Masood a name as one of the best guerrilla generals in the 13-year war against the communist government.
He became defence minister in the guerrilla government that ousted the one led by former president Najibullah in 1992, three years after Soviet forces quit Afghanistan.
Since his retreat to the Panjsher, Masood has been working hard to organise its defence against the Taleban, his men say.

They have used dynamite to bring landslides across a narrow road that runs by a swift-flowing river into the Panjsher to try to stop tanks or other vehicles from advancing into a valley where Masood is said to have stocked fuel, ammunition and food.

He imposed a state of emergency on the valley and ordered non-combatants to leave, sending a stream of women, children and old people trying to clamber to safety along a narrow, rock-strewn path that clings to one side of the treeless gorge.

Soviet-built helicopter gunships launched rockets into the valley, but came under fire from Masood's men. As dusk fell, more Taleban fighters moved into the valley, but appeared to be facing stiff resistance.
One Taleban commander yelled into his walkie-talkie for the barrage to stop after rockets hit hillsides his men had already taken.
Taleban commander Ali Jay said his forces had sustained no casualties during the 12-hour-old assault.

The Taleban leadership have said they will not deal with Masood, but have been anxious to talk peace with another potential foe, Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who controls six northern provinces from the city of Mazar-i-Sharif.
The Taleban say they have no quarrel with Dostum, a former communist general who switched sides just before Najibullah's government collapsed, and are prepared to negotiate with him.
There has been no firm word of talks so far, but Dostum has massed tanks and other heavy military equipment south of the Salang Tunnel, some 90 km (60 miles) north of Kabul.
The Salang is a major choke point on the road from Kabul through the Hindu Kush mountains to Mazar-i-Sharif and on to Central Asia.
The Uzbeks, widely regarded as some of the best fighters in Afghanistan, practice a much more liberal version of Islam than the Taleban, who have begun imposing a strict Islamic order on the country.
One Uzbek officer told Reuters in the Salang Pass that Dostum's army was ready to fight the Taleban if they tried to force their way into the north.
